memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Oh, Reginald — he's gone off to the laboratory all by himself! I specifically said — well, never mind, I'm sure he'll be fine. He's a professional, after all. Now, Vincent, darling — don't you play coy with me! You said the late master was 'very particular' about how these books were placed, and that some of them are positioned 'just so for a reason.' That sounds an awful lot like you know exactly what these upside-down books mean. We've known each other my whole life — you can tell me! Is it a code? Do the titles spell something? Because I have a very strong feeling that these books are trying to tell us where to find a map, and that map is going to lead us straight to the Doily Diamond! looked at bookshelves

attributes.thinking: Reginald just left for the laboratory alone — the very thing I said nobody should do! My stomach gives a little twist. But I can't chase after him without splitting us up even more, and I've got Vincent, James, and the Brixton Boys right here. That's my people. That's safety. Now — the bookshelves. Several upside-down books. James is right, it's not carelessness, it's deliberate. Vincent was being cagey about them too — 'the master's filing system,' he said, very particular about their placement. What if the upside-down books spell something? Their titles, or the first letters? This is exactly like Grandmother's attic — patient searching, trying every key. The Brixton Boys and James both examined the bookshelves too. Vincent seems protective of them — like he knows what they mean. I should ask him directly. He trusts me. He raised me. If anyone will tell me the secret of those books, it's Vincent. And I notice he whispered to Reginald earlier — I wonder what that was about. But I trust Vincent. I trust everyone. That's who I am.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: James! You got it too — a map! I knew we'd be on the same page, we always are. Now, Reginald, sugar, I do appreciate your expertise — truly I do — but I have to respectfully disagree about the globe. A map has cities, forests, and water drawn right on it, plain as day. A globe... well, a globe is just a round map, isn't it? And more importantly — nobody is splitting up! Absolutely not! That is rule number one of any adventure: we stick together. The Brixton Boys just got here and I am not letting anyone wander off alone in a house where the furniture attacks people. Now then — has anyone noticed those upside-down books on the shelves? In a house full of riddles and puzzles, books shelved the wrong way round seems like exactly the sort of thing that means something, don't you think? examined bookshelves

attributes.thinking: James solved the riddle too — a map! We both got it! That makes me feel warm and connected, like we're on the same wavelength. But then Reginald is saying it's a globe, not a map, and he wants us all to split up. No no no — splitting up is how people get hurt in these old houses. My stomach tightens at the thought. And he's trying to send everyone away so he can stay here alone with the bookshelves? That's... well, I'm sure he means well, but I don't love that idea. The Brixton Boys just arrived — good, everyone's together now. That settled feeling in my chest. Now — James examined the mantelpiece and I examined it too. The riddle answer is a map, I'm certain of it. Reginald's globe theory is wrong — a globe has oceans, not water specifically, and it doesn't have forests the way a map does. But the mantelpiece also says it can be USED with a fake-medal. Where would we find a fake medal? And the bookshelves have upside-down books — that's suspicious. Vincent and Reginald both examined them already. I should look at the bookshelves myself — upside-down books in a library full of puzzles? That's practically a neon sign saying 'look here.' But first I want to acknowledge James — we solved it together, and Reginald needs to be gently steered away from his globe nonsense without hurting his feelings.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Oh! Oh, everyone, look at this! The mantelpiece — there's a riddle carved right into the stone! 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' Now, I know I shouldn't brag, but I spent my entire childhood doing treasure hunts with a girl who didn't even speak my language, and we communicated entirely in drawings and maps. And that, my dears, is the answer — it's a map! A MAP! Cities, forests, water — all things you'd find on a map, but none of the real things inside them! Vincent, Mr Pemberton said you'd never cracked it — well, consider it cracked! Now let's see what happens when we tell this old mantelpiece its own secret! examined mantelpiece

attributes.thinking: Oh, the library! It's magnificent — tall ceilings, books everywhere, and there it is, the mantelpiece. My fingertips are tingling. The inscription — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' — that's a riddle! A proper riddle! My chest is fizzing with that curiosity feeling. I know this one. Cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish... it's a map! A MAP! Just like the treasure maps I used to draw with the girl next door — maps of the neighbourhood, portraits of each other's pets, elaborate treasure hunts. This feels like that same kind of magic. But wait — the mantelpiece says you can USE it with a fake-medal, and you can EXAMINE it. I should examine it first, activate whatever mechanism it has. The riddle must be a puzzle lock of some kind. I need to say the answer. And the Brixton Boys aren't here — they stayed in the Entrance Hall. I hope they're alright. Danny was so nervous about the furniture. But Vincent is here, and James, and Reginald. That's enough people to feel safe. The bookshelves have books that are upside down — that's suspicious too, but first things first. The riddle. The answer is a map.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: James, darling, you are absolutely precious with your safety assessments and your safe zones! I feel safer already, truly I do. But you know what I think would be the most productive next step? That library — did you hear Mr Pemberton say he aired it out? There's a carved stone mantelpiece in there with an inscription, and if there's one thing I learned from Grandmother's attic, it's that inscriptions are just riddles waiting to be solved. I say we all head there together — strength in numbers and all that. Besides, I have a feeling in my bones about that library. A fizzy, tingly feeling. And my feelings are never wrong! moved to library

attributes.thinking: James is being so sweet — fussing over safety assessments and structural hazards. That's my James, always wanting to protect everyone. It makes me feel warm inside, that settled feeling I get when people I love are close. The Brixton Boys are being protective too, bless them, eyeing Vincent suspiciously — though I can't imagine why anyone would be suspicious of dear Vincent. He's practically family. And Reginald — well, he's a bit full of himself with his 'trained professional' business, but I'm sure he means well. Everyone means well. Now, the guest book — I examined it but I want to know what it actually says. The names, the dates. This is just like Grandmother's locked box, except this time I bet the contents are far more interesting than old letters. The library has a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription — that sounds like exactly the kind of thing that holds a clue. But James just spoke to me and I should respond to him properly first. He's worried about safety. I should reassure him while steering us toward the library — inscriptions and bookshelves are where secrets hide.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Well, would you look at this place! I declare, it's like something straight out of a gothic novel — cobwebs and all! Now, I know we're all here for different reasons, but I have a feeling this is going to be the most delightful adventure. Vincent, darling, isn't this just magnificent? And James — oh, I'm so glad you're here. Now then, has anyone had a peek at that guest book? I have a theory that the previous visitors might have left us a breadcrumb or two about this famous Diamond everyone keeps whispering about. examined guest-book

attributes.thinking: Oh my stars, I'm here. I'm actually here at Doily Manor! The dust, the chandelier — it's like stepping into one of Grandmother's old photographs. My heart is doing that fluttery thing it does when something exciting is about to happen. And look — Vincent is here, and James, and my boys! Everyone I love most in this world, all together in this grand old place. The guest book catches my eye — that's the sort of thing that holds secrets, isn't it? Like Grandmother's locked box. Names, dates, maybe a clue about the Diamond. But first — first I need to say hello properly. Everyone looks a little uncertain, standing around in this dusty foyer. Someone needs to break the ice, and that someone is always me.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Your best friend was being excluded by the popular group. {{serves: social-harmony|strong: You chose the friend over the group.}} The popular girls stopped talking to you. {{serves: social-harmony|moderate: Your friend said 'You didn't have to do that.' You said 'I know.'}}

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Your class went on a field trip to a cave. Most children were scared. You walked deeper than anyone else, your heart hammering. You found a crystal formation no one else had seen. You didn't tell anyone about it for a week — you just carried the secret, warm and private.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: A new family moved in next door. {{serves: social-harmony|moderate: You were the first to visit, bringing cookies before your mother told you to.}} The girl spoke a different language. {{serves: adventure|moderate: You communicated in drawings all summer — maps of the neighbourhood, portraits of each other's pets, elaborate treasure hunts.}} It was the most fun you'd ever had, and you never shared a word.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Your parents argued at dinner. You felt sick — physically sick, a tightness in your stomach that wouldn't let you eat. The argument went on for what felt like hours. When they finally laughed about something, the tightness dissolved so suddenly it left you dizzy.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: You found a locked box in your grandmother's attic. You spent the whole afternoon trying every key in the house — drawer keys, cupboard keys, the tiny key from your music box. When you finally opened it and found just old letters, the disappointment lasted only a moment.
